nameStory: The Canadian Flat-back Millipede gets its name from two key features: its distinctly flattened body shape (unlike the cylindrical pill bugs you might know) and its northern range that extends well into Canada. The 'flat-back' part is literal - these millipedes look like they've been gently pressed down, giving them a broad, ribbon-like appearance as they crawl through leaf litter.
description: The Canadian Flat-back Millipede is a small, segmented creature that looks like a tiny brown ribbon with legs crawling through the forest floor. Unlike their round cousins, these millipedes have distinctly flattened bodies with wing-like extensions called keels along their sides. They're typically less than an inch long and move with a gentle, wave-like motion as their many legs work in coordination. Despite their name suggesting otherwise, millipedes don't actually have a thousand legs - this species has around 30-40 pairs depending on its age.

idTips.label: Black stripe down the back
idTips.description: Look for a distinctive dark line running down the center of the back from head to tail - this stripe feels smooth to the touch and is the best way to distinguish it from similar species

idTips.label: Flattened, ribbon-like body
idTips.description: The body feels firm but flexible, like a thin leather strap, and appears pressed flat rather than round when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Wing-like side projections
idTips.description: Small, thin flaps extend from each body segment along the sides, giving it a slightly broader appearance and helping it wedge under bark and leaves

idTips.label: Brown coloration with lighter edges
idTips.description: The overall color is earthy brown, often with slightly paler margins along the sides that contrast with the dark central stripe

idTips.label: Slow, undulating movement
idTips.description: Moves with a gentle wave-like motion rather than quick scurrying, and will curl into a loose spiral when disturbed

habitat: You'll find Canadian Flat-back Millipedes in moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly under rotting logs, leaf litter, and loose bark. They prefer areas with rich, organic soil that stays consistently damp, often in maple, oak, and birch woodlands. Look for them in the same spots where you might find salamanders - cool, humid microhabitats away from direct sunlight.

seasonality.spring: Most active as soil warms and becomes workable again. Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and are often found under fresh fallen logs and stones.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're easiest to spot during the day under cover. Young millipedes appear, looking like miniature versions of adults but with fewer body segments.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move deeper into soil and more secure winter hideouts. Often found in deeper leaf litter as they prepare for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Inactive and hidden deep in soil, under logs, or in other protected spots. Rarely seen unless you're doing serious digging in unfrozen ground.

funFact: When threatened, this millipede can actually 'sweat' a smelly, slightly toxic liquid from pores along its sides - the fluid has a distinctive almond-like odor that some people find surprisingly pleasant, while others compare it to cherry cough drops!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the Common Pink Flat-back Millipede, but the Canadian species has that telltale black stripe down its back while the Common Pink Flat-back lacks this stripe entirely. Memory trick: 'Canadian stripe' - Canadians wear distinctive striped hockey jerseys!
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - millipedes are actually beneficial decomposers, not pests. Unlike centipedes (which are predators with one pair of legs per segment), millipedes are gentle vegetarians with two pairs of legs per segment who help break down dead plant material into rich soil.
compareHints: The Canadian Flat-back is easily separated from its close relative, the Common Pink Flat-back Millipede, by that distinctive black mid-dorsal stripe running down its back. Both species share the same flattened body shape and similar size, but only the Canadian species sports this dark racing stripe. If you see a flat-backed millipede without the stripe, you've likely found the Common Pink Flat-back instead.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Common Pink Flat-back is distinguished from its close relative, the Canadian Flat-back Millipede, primarily by its consistent pink coloration and slightly smaller size.
